course.title: QuickBite — Software Engineering Laboratory
course.summary: One continuous engineering project across 20 laboratory sessions. Your project folder is the working repository: reports, models, experiments, code and test evidence travel with it.

scenario.problem: QuickBite is a proposed food-ordering and delivery service. The company wants one digital flow for placing, fulfilling and tracking orders, but the brief intentionally leaves important engineering decisions open.
brief_points: Local restaurants currently use different ways to receive and confirm orders, which makes the customer experience inconsistent.
Customers need clearer information about whether an order was accepted, prepared, handed to delivery and completed.
Restaurants need a workable way to accept or reject incoming orders and communicate fulfilment status.
Delivery work must be coordinated with restaurant readiness without building a real route-optimization or GPS platform.
Payment and notification capabilities may be provided by external services; QuickBite should coordinate with them rather than implement real payment processing.
The teaching project uses synthetic data. Your team must decide and justify many details instead of trying to guess one hidden solution.

modules.title: Project vision, software process and feasibility
theory: Software engineering addresses the complete production and evolution of professional software, not only coding.
A software process normally includes specification, design/implementation, validation and evolution.
Process models are abstractions: sequential, iterative, incremental and risk-driven approaches emphasize different ways to organize work.
A project vision links a stakeholder problem to measurable outcomes, scope, assumptions and constraints.
Feasibility asks whether the proposal is technically, operationally, economically and schedule-wise credible.
steps: Read the QuickBite scenario and separate information you can treat as given from assumptions and unresolved questions.
Write a concise problem statement and project vision. Avoid implementation technologies unless they are genuine constraints.
Identify stakeholders yourself. For each, record a need, a concern and one question that would reduce uncertainty.
Define project scope and explicit exclusions. Justify at least one boundary decision that could reasonably have been made differently.
Create three measurable business objectives. State how each could be measured and which values are assumptions rather than observed data.
Compare at least two lifecycle approaches and justify how you would organize this project. A hybrid is allowed if you can defend it.
Use the feasibility simulator for a base case and two sensitivity scenarios of your own choosing. Explain why you changed those inputs.
Prepare technical, operational, economic and schedule feasibility plus an initial risk register. Finish with GO, CONDITIONAL GO or NO-GO and justify it.
checks: Can another person distinguish facts from assumptions?
Do objectives measure outcomes rather than merely list features?
Is the lifecycle choice justified by project conditions?
Does feasibility acknowledge uncertainty rather than treating simulator output as proof?
outcomes: Describe and compare common lifecycle approaches.
Create an initial project vision and feasibility study.
modules.challenge: Build a defensible case for what problem QuickBite should solve, for whom, and under what boundaries. Do not start by inventing features.

work: Read the scenario without jumping to a solution.
Draft the problem statement and vision.
Define scope, exclusions and measurable objectives.
before_leave: Export the complete project ZIP and store it outside the lab computer.

modules.title: Requirements engineering and traceability
theory: Requirements engineering includes elicitation, analysis, specification, validation and management.
Business requirements describe organizational outcomes; functional requirements describe system services; non-functional requirements define measurable quality/operational constraints.
Acceptance criteria make requirements testable.
Traceability links goals, requirements, models and tests so change impact can be analyzed.
steps: Review M01 and identify information that should become requirements, assumptions or unresolved questions.
Create a requirements register containing business, functional and non-functional requirements. Choose a reasonable decomposition and justify it.
For every requirement record a stable ID, source, priority, rationale and acceptance criterion.
Check whether the set covers the end-to-end service across ordering, fulfilment, delivery and relevant external interactions without copying a predefined feature list.
Define measurable quality constraints for the areas that matter to this project and explain why each metric is meaningful.
Write several user-oriented requirements and add normal plus failure/boundary acceptance scenarios.
Create a traceability baseline from business goals to requirements and planned downstream evidence.
Peer-review ambiguous or compound requirements. Preserve at least three before/after revisions.
checks: Does each requirement express one main obligation?
Are NFRs objectively verifiable?
Can important requirements be traced to a goal/source?
Are planned tests/models clearly distinguished from executed evidence?
outcomes: Establish traceability and a change baseline.
modules.challenge: Translate the project vision into a coherent requirements baseline without letting the task description design the system for you.

modules.title: Use cases and activity modeling
theory: Use cases capture actor goals at the system boundary; the detailed textual use case carries behavior that the diagram alone cannot show.
Activity diagrams model workflow, decisions, merges and concurrent paths.
Models are abstractions and must remain consistent with requirements.
steps: Identify the external actors relevant to your requirements baseline and decide which goals deserve use cases.
Create a use-case model with a clear system boundary and goal-level names. Justify any external system modeled as an actor.
Write one complete textual use case for an important interaction, including meaningful alternative and failure flows.
Create an activity model for a workflow where branching matters. Make guards explicit and avoid invented concurrency.
Walk through success plus two non-success scenarios using only the model and specification.
Trace modeled behavior back to M02 and note anything missing, duplicated or inconsistent.
Ask another team to follow the specification without verbal help and record the first ambiguity they find.
checks: Are actors external to the system?
Are use cases goals rather than UI controls?
Do activity decisions have meaningful guards/outcomes?
Can reviewers trace modeled behavior to requirements?
outcomes: Build use case and activity models.
Specify a use case in text.
modules.challenge: Choose which user goals and workflows are important enough to model. The starter diagrams provide notation, not the QuickBite answer.

modules.title: Structured analysis and information flow
theory: A context diagram treats the system as one process and shows external information flows.
A DFD decomposes transformations, external entities and data stores.
A data dictionary defines shared information structures.
Access analysis separates who may read/change which information.
steps: Derive external information exchanges from existing requirements and create a context-level model.
Decompose the system into a small number of meaningful transformations and relevant data stores.
Check balancing between context and level-1 views. Explain any renamed or aggregated flow.
Create a data dictionary for the core information structures your models rely on.
Create an access matrix for relevant roles and information resources. Justify at least one denied operation.
Analyze one information-flow risk and propose a control plus a way to verify it.
Compare the DFD with your activity model: what does each reveal and intentionally omit?
checks: Do external flows cross the boundary consistently?
Are stores accessed through processes?
Are data names consistent across artifacts?
Does risk analysis connect asset, control and verification?
outcomes: Model system context and information flow.
Reason about access and data exposure.
modules.challenge: Model how information moves through QuickBite without turning the DFD into a flowchart or copying implementation architecture.

modules.title: Reliability, availability, fault tolerance and security
theory: Reliability is continuity of correct service over time; availability is readiness for use at a given time.
Redundancy can improve availability but introduces assumptions such as independent failures and successful failover.
RTO describes the maximum acceptable recovery time; RPO describes acceptable data-loss time.
Security engineering identifies assets, threats, trust boundaries, controls and residual risk.
steps: Identify service failures that would meaningfully affect stakeholders and distinguish reliability from availability concerns.
Define or refine measurable dependability requirements and state their assumptions.
Use the availability simulator for a base scenario and at least two alternatives that answer a question you formulate.
Describe one fault-tolerance or recovery strategy and explain which failure it addresses—and which it does not.
Identify important assets and plausible threats. Prioritize a manageable subset rather than a generic threat list.
For each selected threat, propose a control and a verification idea. Discuss one trade-off introduced by a control.
Update risks/requirements where the analysis reveals new constraints.
checks: Are reliability and availability used correctly?
Are simulator assumptions documented?
Does each control address a specific threat?
Can claims be connected to planned evidence?
outcomes: Create a basic threat model and security verification plan.
modules.challenge: Decide which failures and threats matter most. Do not treat a single simulator percentage as proof.

modules.title: Architecture, physical infrastructure and deployment
theory: Architecture structures the system so functional and non-functional requirements can be achieved.
Layered architecture separates interface, application, domain and infrastructure concerns.
Deployment models map software artifacts and execution environments to physical or virtual nodes.
Capacity estimates are planning aids, not response-time proof.
steps: Identify architectural responsibilities implied by requirements and quality constraints.
Propose a logical architecture and justify how responsibilities are separated. Compare at least one alternative/trade-off.
Create a package/component-style view using the simplified notation or an external CASE tool.
Design a deployment view showing the execution environment and external dependencies relevant to the project.
Use the capacity simulator to explore at least two demand/failure scenarios. Interpret results as estimates.
Record one architecture decision in ADR-style form: context, decision, alternatives and consequences.
Review whether architecture/deployment address earlier NFRs.
checks: Are responsibilities clear rather than just technology names?
Are dependencies understandable?
Is deployment distinct from logical design?
Are capacity results described as estimates?
outcomes: Relate architecture to NFRs and operations.
modules.challenge: Design architecture that explains responsibility and deployment without assuming the tool starter is the desired solution.

modules.title: Class modeling and design patterns
theory: Class diagrams model structural concepts, attributes, operations and relationships.
Multiplicity expresses how many instances may participate in an association.
Creational, structural and behavioral patterns solve recurring design pressures; pattern use should be justified by context, not by name-dropping.
steps: Identify candidate domain concepts from requirements, use cases and information models. Remove duplicates and UI-only concepts.
Create a class model with meaningful responsibilities and relationships. Add multiplicities where they matter.
Explain at least two non-obvious modeling choices.
Identify one design problem where a pattern could help. Compare at least two approaches before selecting a pattern.
Model relevant packages/dependencies and check for unnecessary coupling.
Walk one change scenario and explain which model elements would need to change.
checks: Do classes represent stable concepts/responsibilities?
Are multiplicities meaningful?
Is the pattern linked to a real design problem?
Are dependencies intentional?
modules.challenge: Derive a domain/design model from requirements and behavior instead of copying nouns from the scenario or starter.

task_specs.complete_when: The final concept list is grounded in prior artifacts and separates domain from interface/implementation concerns.

modules.title: Sequence and state modeling
theory: Sequence diagrams show participants and ordered interactions for a scenario.
State machines show valid object histories through states and event-triggered transitions.
A scenario must be compatible with both actor permissions and the state model.
steps: Choose one behaviorally important scenario and identify participants needed to realize it.
Create a sequence model showing credible message order; describe at least one alternative/error case in text.
Identify a stateful concept whose legal lifecycle matters and define its states/transitions.
Create a state machine and document invalid/forbidden transitions that matter to correctness.
Cross-check sequence messages against class/package responsibilities and requirements.
Walk one requirement change through both dynamic models and note inconsistencies.
checks: Does the sequence explain responsibility rather than UI clicks?
Are state transitions event-driven/legal?
Are terminal/forbidden cases explicit?
Do dynamic models agree with earlier artifacts?
modules.challenge: Choose representative scenarios and lifecycle behavior. Starter notation should not decide your participants, messages or states.

before_leave: Submit only if requested as a checkpoint.

modules.title: CASE tools, planning, change and professional practice
theory: CASE tools support creation, maintenance and checking of engineering artifacts but do not replace semantic review.
A backlog organizes outcomes and dependencies.
Change management uses traceability to identify affected requirements, models, code and tests.
Professional practice requires honest evidence, transparent limitations and accountable contributions.
steps: Audit the project repository for missing, duplicated or inconsistent evidence and record issues.
Create a short project plan for remaining work with milestones, dependencies and responsibilities.
Process a change request that affects an existing rule. Identify impacted requirements, models, code/tests and evidence before deciding.
Update affected artifacts while preserving the reason for change and previous baseline where appropriate.
Analyze one professional/ethical issue raised by the system/change. Identify affected stakeholders and competing obligations.
Perform a repository review with another team and record one improvement.
checks: Can a reviewer see why an artifact changed?
Does change impact follow traceability?
Are milestones tied to deliverables/evidence?
Does ethical analysis consider affected people?
outcomes: Analyze change impact and professional evidence.
modules.challenge: Treat the repository as a connected engineering record. Use tools to expose reasoning, not to produce diagrams for their own sake.

modules.title: Software testing, Python defect repair and release
theory: Testing levels include unit, integration, system and acceptance testing; levels answer where testing occurs while techniques such as boundary analysis answer how cases are chosen.
A useful test has an independent expected result derived from a requirement or contract.
Defect repair follows reproduce → isolate → fix → regression.
A release candidate links requirements, models, code and executed evidence while keeping known limitations visible.
steps: Create a small test strategy covering appropriate levels and the most important requirements/risk areas.
Design test cases using normal, boundary, invalid and state-transition reasoning. Link them to requirement IDs.
Open the Python laboratory and inspect the published function contracts in the editable implementation file.
Before revealing supplied tests, add your own tests for at least three contract behaviors and run only your student test file.
Then reveal and run the supplied regression tests. Treat failures as mismatches to investigate, not instructions to edit tests.
Repair defects in student_code/policies.py one at a time. Preserve evidence of at least one failing and corresponding passing run.
Run the complete suite, update defect notes and summarize residual limitations.
Prepare an integrated release review: what is verified, what remains assumed, and whether you would release.
checks: Do expected results come from requirements/contracts?
Are boundary/invalid cases represented?
Were supplied tests left unchanged?
Does release status distinguish evidence from assumption?
outcomes: Use Python unit tests to reproduce and repair defects.
Produce a reproducible evidence-based release package.
modules.challenge: Use requirements as the source of expected behavior. Write your own tests before revealing the supplied regression suite.

session_plan.focus: Test design and independent student tests
